# How the numbers were made {#sec-appD}

Several of this book's most quotable figures are not measurements. They are constructions: a
coefficient applied to an area, a ratio inferred from a handful of texts, a total extrapolated from
one surviving document. Where a chapter needs the finding but not the derivation, the derivation
lives here, so that a reader who wants to know how confident to be can see the working.

The rule this appendix applies throughout: a number built by multiplying an uncertain quantity by an
assumed coefficient inherits the uncertainty of both, and the range it spans is usually wider than
the debate about it suggests.

## How urbanisation rates get made, and why two experts differ by a factor of three

The share of a population living in cities is one of the most-used numbers in economic history, and
in the deep past it is manufactured rather than counted. Mesopotamia offers an unusually clean
demonstration, because two respected reconstructions of the same society disagree by a factor of
three and the disagreement is entirely methodological.

Robert McC. Adams, working from archaeological survey, estimated that by about 2400 BCE some 78 per
cent of the Sumerian population lived in settlements larger than 40 hectares — an extraordinarily
urbanised society by any pre-modern standard. Piotr Steinkeller, working from the place-names
recorded in administrative texts, reached the opposite conclusion for Ur III Umma: 70 to 80 per cent
of its people lived outside the city, where Adams's survey figures implied about 25 per cent.

Neither is careless. Survey finds sites by walking the ground and reading potsherds, and in an
alluvial floodplain small settlements are buried, scoured away or hidden under later silt, so survey
systematically under-counts the countryside. Texts record the places an administration had reason to
name, which is not the same as the places people lived. Emberling attributes part of the gap to the
two methods covering different time spans and part to sites the survey simply missed.

The lesson generalises, and this book will need it repeatedly. An urbanisation rate is a ratio of
two constructed quantities, and the method that built each one determines the answer. When Chapter 2
takes up the population of Pataliputra, the same problem appears in a different guise: there the
disagreement is not between survey and texts but between two lines drawn on the same site plan.

One further figure from the same chapter is worth holding beside these. Tell Brak, in northern Syria
some 750 kilometres from Uruk, had reached about 130 hectares of settled area before 3500 BCE,
perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people, and it was contemporary with the southern cities rather than derived
from them. Any account that makes southern irrigation the cause of Mesopotamian urbanism has to
explain the north as well.

*Sources: Emberling, "Mesopotamian cities and urban process, 3500-1600 BCE", in* The Cambridge World
History*, vol. 3 (2015), pp. 253-78, at pp. 271-72 for the Adams and Steinkeller figures and his
account of the discrepancy, p. 275 for Ur at not much more than 50 hectares while the Wool Office
employed some 13,000 workers, p. 262 for Tell Brak, and p. 255 for dry farming constraining northern
cities to roughly 100 hectares until Neo-Assyrian irrigation.*

*Chapter 1 keeps the finding — that urbanisation rates are constructions rather than observations,
and that two careful scholars can differ by a factor of three — and sends the derivation here.*


## How big was Pataliputra? A number and its pedigree

Figures between 40,000 and 400,000 circulate for Mauryan Pataliputra. Following one of them back is
a short course in how ancient quantities are made.

The chain begins with Megasthenes, the Seleucid ambassador to Chandragupta, who described the city
in his *Indica*. That book is lost. What survives are passages quoted by Strabo and Arrian
centuries later, and the version most often cited is McCrindle's translation of 1877. Through them
Megasthenes gives dimensions: a parallelogram some eighty stadia long and fifteen broad, girded by a
timber wall with 570 towers and sixty-four gates, and a ditch that doubled as the sewer.

Converted, that is roughly nine miles by two. But converted into what *area*? Here the estimates
part company, and by more than is usually admitted. Allchin offers two: about 2,200 hectares for
the outer rampart circuit, or about 340 hectares for the ground enclosed by the city moat. Erdosy
gives a rampart-based range topping out at 1,350 hectares — often quoted alongside the others as
if it were a third independent survey, which it is not. And Allchin reports Erdosy again, at 4,500
hectares, for the area Megasthenes's description actually implies.

The last step is a density assumption. The standard coefficient is 120 persons per hectare — a
figure Robert McC. Adams derived for Mesopotamia, and which Erdosy then imported into South Asia.
Multiply it out and the arithmetic is unforgiving:

| Area used | × 120 per hectare | Population |
|---|---|---|
| 340 ha (inside the moat) | | ~41,000 |
| 1,200–1,350 ha (rampart circuit, Erdosy) | | ~144,000–162,000 |
| 2,200 ha (outer ramparts, Allchin) | | ~264,000 |
| 4,500 ha (the area Megasthenes implies) | | ~540,000 |

Nothing separates these answers except a decision about which line on the ground counts as the
city. Same lost text, same translation, same coefficient, same modern authorities cited at more
than one point on the range — and a spread of about thirteen to one. It is worth being clear what
that does to the figures in general circulation: the familiar "about 200,000" needs no unaudited
source to explain it, because it falls inside a range the held literature generates on its own. Shonaleeka Kaul, writing the *Cambridge World History* study of the
city, takes the moat figure and concludes that "well over 40,000" people lived there, calling even
that conservative.

Set against this, what has actually been dug is a thin record. Pataliputra lies beneath modern Patna;
dense settlement and a high water table have kept excavation to fragments. The wooden palisade at
Bulandibagh — plausibly Megasthenes' wall — has been traced for about 350 feet. There is a burnt
pillared hall at Kumrahar whose function is disputed three ways. That is the physical record for
the greatest city in India.

None of this means the city was small. Every comparison in the table below survives the
uncertainty, because the same conventions were applied to all of them, and on any reading
Pataliputra was far larger than any other South Asian city of its day. It means that the number
is an artefact of method, and that a book which quotes one figure without its boundary assumption
has told you less than it appears to.

| City | Enclosed area |
|---|---|
| Pataliputra | 340 ha (moat) to 2,200 ha (ramparts) |
| Rajagriha, the old Magadhan capital | up to 240 ha |
| Toshali (Sisupalgarh) | up to 180 ha |
| Ujjayini | 120 ha |
| Taxila | 60 ha |
| *Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, for comparison* | *c. 85 ha each* |

The Harappan row needs a warning, and it is the same warning as the rest of this section. That c. 85
hectares is Kaul and Allchin's own comparator, on their own convention, which is what makes the
column internally consistent. It is not the figure Chapter 1 uses: there Mohenjo-daro is above 200
hectares, in the same class as Uruk rather than a third of it. The two numbers measure different
things --- an occupied mound against a wider site extent --- so the cross-period comparison inherits
a boundary problem at *both* ends, and cannot carry a precise multiple.

*Sources: Kaul, "Regional study: Pataliputra", in* The Cambridge World History*, vol. 4 (2015), pp.
514–36; Allchin,* The Archaeology of Early Historic South Asia *(1995), pp. 109, 202, and ch. 3 for
the comparative areas; Adams,* Heartland of Cities *(1981), for the density coefficient.*

*Chapter 2 keeps the finding --- that the answer moves by a factor of about six and a half on
a single decision about which line on the ground counts as the city, and that the hierarchy is
secure where the number is not --- and sends the derivation here.*
